highlights:
## October 8, 2026

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

# The average customer now saves 25% with SFC#

September 9, 2026

The average customer now saves 25%

Evan Conrad CEO

Today, on-platform customers on SFC receive an average 25% realized discount off their compute price, via resale.

That means a customer buying $100k of compute receives $25k back from selling idle capacity, on average. For a customer who bought at $4.50/GPU/hr, that brings their realized price to $3.375/GPU/hr.

Purchased / GPU hr$4.500

→

Realized / GPU hr$4.500

Recovered 0%

## How to maximize your utilization#

To maximize your realized price per GPU hour, SFC implements an order book that lets you get reserved capacity and then sell that capacity later. This lets you safely buy larger quantities, increasing your revenue, without taking the catastrophic risk that other locked in, long term contracts allow.

For most customers, this process is automatic. If you don’t want your node, just turn it off.

However, this article shows how some folks maximally use SFC to maximize their utilization, snatch up very cheap compute, and reduce their overall risk. It walks through how we built givemeanode, our autoresearch product, on top of SFC as a market maker.

...

The examples below build up this process, one decision at a time. Each node has eight GPUs. The treasury limits each order to 24 hours, but delivery can be many days away. The six-month view above shows the broader planning idea.

Prices and budgets below are example values. They are not live quotes or givemeanode's settings. Each purchase or sale is a separate example.

...

## 2. Compare prices for the same hours#

A bid is an offer to buy. An ask is an offer to sell. Both specify a price and a delivery window.

The treasury reads prices for each eligible SKU. It selects the lowest ask within its buy limit. All candidates must meet the work's hardware needs.

In use Resold Bought Idle

$16 is the lowest ask · limit $18 / node-hour

Here, SKU B costs $16 per node-hour. It is cheaper than SKU A at $18. When prices change, SKU A becomes the next choice.

...

This buy order requests one node for 12 hours. Its $18 limit is per node-hour, or $2.25 per GPU-hour for this eight-GPU node. Its maximum cost is $216.

## October 13, 2026

1. 20:00 UTC

### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

You say to your agent

> “Is the price of an H100 going to change soon?”

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

When we schedule an increase, the dashboard shows a notice until a few days after it takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used that type in the last 90 days get an email.

Your agent sees it too. Until the increase takes effect, `create_node` and `get_node` carry it in `rate.upcoming_increase`, and `submit_job` carries it in `upcoming_increase`. The field gives the time it takes effect, the new list rate per GPU and per node, and the new discounts. A running node also gets a `price_change` event on `/v1/events`. See Rates.

## August 31, 2026

1. 23:30 UTC

### Rollout sandboxes are now just sandboxes

What we called rollout sandboxes is now just sandboxes, in the docs, in the pricing table on the front page, on your usage page, and on your invoice. A rollout is one thing you can run in a sandbox. Plenty of you run agent tool calls, builds, and untrusted code in them instead, and the shorter name covers all of it.

Nothing else moved. Every call, parameter, and id is unchanged, the rates are the same, and the docs section keeps its address. Three labels read differently. The two pricing rows are now Sandboxes (active) and Sandboxes (parked), and the line on your usage page and your invoice is Sandboxes. If a script of yours matches on those strings, that is the one thing to update.

results.title: Run agent-driven experiments with SF Autoresearch | SF Compute
results.author: San Francisco Compute
highlights:
# Run agent-driven experiments with SF Autoresearch#

September 11, 2026

Introducing SF Autoresearch

San Francisco Compute

Today, San Francisco Compute (SFC) announces SF Autoresearch, a platform as a service (PaaS) built for autoresearch and agent-driven experimentation. Give your agent compute, an objective, and a way to measure progress. It can run experiments, compare results, and choose what to try next. Start from your terminal, connect your own agent, or request access to our managed research agents.

...

Create an H100 node and check its GPU:

```
autor node create --name first-experiment --chip h100 --wait
autor run first-experiment -- nvidia-smi
```

The `--wait` flag waits for capacity. `nvidia-smi` reports the GPU your code can use. When you finish, stop compute billing and keep the node’s files:

```
autor node stop first-experiment
```

...

## Scale through SFC’s order book#

Autoresearch buys compute through SFC’s order book, a physically settled market where customers buy and resell GPU capacity. SFC operates every cluster it sells capacity on. That gives you a path from one experiment to thousands of GPUs without a long-term capacity commitment. Scale independent experiments and batch jobs across the fleet as capacity becomes available.

SFC’s upcoming deployments will expand that supply. The same market connects Autoresearch to capacity from the new clusters coming online, so your experiments can grow with the fleet.
